newsitem.title: USA: China, ex-Soviets must curb ag trade monopoly - US.
newsitem.headline: China, ex-Soviets must curb ag trade monopoly - US.

text.p: China and former republics of the Soviet Union inspire U.S. concern over unfair agricultural trade monopolies, as do marketing boards in Canada, Australia and New Zealand, Deputy Agriculture Secretary Richard Rominger said Thursday.

The United States has made reforms of so-called state trading enterprises (STEs) a priority for world trade negotiations due to begin in 1999 and for a summit by national trade leaders this winter to lay the framework for the global talks.
"If we are to continue to phase out (farm) export subsidies, we need equivalent disciplines on STEs and related trade-distorting practices," Rominger told the House Agriculture Committee.

U.S. officials say STEs, which often enjoy monopoly control over the export of a commodity and operate in secret, can offer unfairly low prices in order to win sales. Other STEs can artificially drive up domestic prices by muzzling imports.

Along with referring to longstanding U.S. concerns with the export dealings of the Canadian Wheat Board, Australian Wheat Board and New Zealand Dairy Board, Rominger said STEs also were a cause for concern in China and former Soviet republics. He said trade practices must be brought under control before the latter nations could join the World Trade Organization.

"Our concerns are shared by other major exporters, including Canada, New Zealand and Australia," Rominger said. "Those common interests regarding...new entrants provide an opportunity, and one of the most compelling arguments we have, for enlisting broader support for efforts to achieve greater transparency and controls with regard to operations of all STEs."

The United States was pursuing a series of alliances to win control of ag-related STEs, according to Rominger and other Agriculture Department officials. It has courted Japan and the European Union for support to rein in exporters like Canada, Australia and New Zealand. But it has made common cause with its ag trade competitors to attack STEs that block imports.

Thirty nations have told the World Trade Organization that a total of 121 STEs were involved in their agricultural trade. STEs were active in grain, dairy, cotton, livestock, meat, oilseeds, horticultural products and some tropical products.
In a statement, the New Zealand Dairy Board said it was a fair trader. It said its profits from sales to the United States stemmed from artificially high U.S. prices.

U.S. farm groups generally backed the Clinton administration in its drive to control STEs. The American Farm Bureau Federation, the largest of the groups, said "we must put China at the top of the list" for use of STEs to block imports.

The National Farmers Union said elimination of STEs would benefit grain processors and exporters while forcing down prices paid to farmers. An end to Canada's Wheat Board, it said, would mean a deluge of grain onto the U.S. market.
